text: Grok Bot is out of beta. Grok Bot 1.0 turns a Bot from a personal assistant into something a whole team can talk to, in the app, in Slack, in Microsoft Teams and in a video call. xAI announced it on November 2, 2026. The app itself got the 1.0 number on November 11. If you’ve never used Grok Bot, start with the deep dive . This post covers only what changed. I run my Bots alone, so I can’t share one with a team. The steps for Team Bots, Slack, Microsoft Teams and meetings follow the documentation, and the screenshots are from the announcement, the changelog and the docs. The announcement is dated November 2 and points to changes that had already shipped in versions 0.71 to 0.75: better browser use, editable Pages, and approvals that ask less often. The changelog lists version 1.0.1 on November 11, and that entry also includes 1.0.0. It is the one that adds meetings, Microsoft Teams, shared connectors and Review learnings . My Mac app was still on 0.79.3 that evening, with the round update button in the sidebar footer. Its tooltip says Restart to update . Check your version before you look for any of the menus below. Shared Bots are called Team Bots again. A few screens still say “shared Bots”, such as Browse shared Bots , and the Team Bots documentation says they’re the same thing. A Team Bot now starts as a draft. Here’s how you create one: Until you publish it, only you can see it. Add only the keys and files you’re happy for every teammate to use, because they work in everyone’s chat. You can still share a Bot you already have. Sharing doesn’t make a copy. Click Share at the top right of the Bot’s chat. Under Who has access you pick your team, your organization, or People you invite . The last one limits the Bot to the people and groups you add under Add people or groups . There are three roles: Copy link gives teammates a link to the same Bot. A template link is different, because it gives each person their own copy. Every teammate’s chat is private. The owner and the Managers can’t read it. This is the part to understand before you put a Bot in a channel. The place where you talk to the Bot decides which computer it uses and whose apps it can reach. In your own chat the Bot asks before it touches your accounts. The card offers Allow once , Always allow and Skip . Approvals follow the person. In a Slack thread the Bot posts a Review an action card, and only the person who asked can answer it. In the beta, a Team Bot saved what it learned for the whole team and told you afterward. In 1.0, when a teammate teaches it something for the team, the Bot suggests the change and waits. The owner and the Managers open the Bot’s details and find Review learnings under Suggested . Each item says what it does, for example Updates the skill , and has Approve and Reject buttons. What the Bot learns about you personally still stays between you and the Bot. Changes the owner or a Manager makes in the main chat apply right away. The same list is in Manage (the wrench icon), under Knowledge . That screen also has Analytics , with messages, hours saved and top users. xAI’s launch note presents Manage as the place to see and steer a Bot’s responsibilities, what it’s learning and its impact. The Bot is also expected to tell you when it’s blocked or confused, and to sum up what it did in a few lines. Slack worked in the beta. Microsoft Teams is new, and it needs three people to say yes: Microsoft doesn’t notify the admin, so send them the link from the dialog. After approval, Teams can take up to an hour to finish the setup. Each person then links their Microsoft account once. Message the Bot and it replies with a Link Account card only you can see. The Microsoft Teams guide has a troubleshooting table for every message the dialog can show. In Teams you mention the Bot in a channel, add it to a group chat, or message it directly. If you ask for a file in a channel, it tells you to message it directly, and sends the file through your OneDrive. The launch note says Bots in Slack and Teams now follow what happens around them, and carry context from one conversation to the next. You can also put more than one Bot in the same thread. xAI says its own Slack has threads where people and several Bots hand off work and decisions to each other. A Bot can join a Google Meet, Zoom or Microsoft Teams call. This one doesn’t need a team, because it’s also on the Ultra plan. Everyone in the call sees who it belongs to. The Bot joins as Bot name (your first name's Bot) - transcribing , or Bot name (Team Bot) - transcribing for a Team Bot. The Bot doesn’t speak. You write to it by name in the meeting chat, and it answers there. If someone asks for something it won’t share with the whole call, it tells you who asked and offers to send it to you. You can ask it questions during the call and assign it action items. xAI says talking back and forth with the Bot live is coming soon. When the call ends, the Bot posts a summary and the action items in its chat. Later you can ask it for the summary or the transcript of any past meeting. The xAI team has a Bot in its standup every day. It writes the notes in a shared Google Doc, and researches the topics that came up. Scheduled meetings show under Upcoming in the Bot’s details. Their menu has Disable Interactivity , which keeps the Bot taking notes without answering, plus Cancel and Quit . A Bot that follows your calendar can also join scheduled meetings on its own. The meetings page has the details. A Team Bot uses the owner’s apps for everyone, and asks before it uses yours. With shared connectors , the owner or a Manager decides this app by app. Open the Bot’s details, then Setup , then Service accounts , and pick an app under Shared connectors : Share your account only works after a team admin turns on Allow Shared Logins , which is off by default. Be careful with it. Whatever the Bot does through that connector, for any teammate, happens as you. The announcement talks a lot about Bots taking initiative. The documentation is more modest about it. Your Primary Bot looks for work it can take over and offers to do it. It also tells you when an app like Gmail signed you out, and offers to reconnect. It offers first, and it still asks before a risky action. A Team Bot can’t be your Primary Bot. What it can do is ask you for something it needs. If a routine needs one of your connected apps, the Team Bot asks in its Slack thread and tags you. You can’t switch the check-ins off yourself. Turning off Notifications for a Bot only silences the alerts. Team admins get a few new switches on the Grok Bot page of the dashboard: The teams and enterprises page lists the rest. Most of 1.0 needs a Team or Enterprise plan. If you use Grok Bot alone, like I do, this is what changes: The 1.0.1 release also has small things for everyone. The Voice menu has a Speed slider from 0.5x to 2x, an expired order card offers Check price again , and the Bot no longer sends a message that only says it’s done. If you work alone, update the app and keep using it as before. On a team, start with one Team Bot for one shared job, shared with People you invite , and look at Review learnings after the first week. Want me to talk about your product?
